PHSCS 587

Image-force barrier lowering

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a field and an attractive image interaction lower a classical barrier

A carrier near an ideal conducting plane polarizes the conductor. In the classical planar model, an electron at distance x in a dielectric of permittivity ε has image interaction energy Uim(x) = −q²/(16πεx). The factor includes the work of building the induced charge distribution. It is an attractive energy correction, measured in joules in SI.

For a positive field magnitude F that lowers the outward barrier, model its energy as U(x) = qφB − qFx − q²/(16πεx). The maximum occurs at xm = √[q/(16πεF)]. Its reduction relative to the unrounded interface barrier is ΔU = qΔφ, where Δφ = √[qF/(4πε)] in volts. Increasing F by four therefore doubles the classical barrier-lowering voltage.

This model assumes an ideal planar metal, a locally uniform field and a continuum dielectric response. Its divergence as x approaches zero signals the failure of that continuum description at atomic distances. Nonplanar contacts, two-dimensional screening and interface chemistry require more detailed models. Image-force lowering is one correction to contact transport, rather than a replacement for the full barrier profile.

Example

A fourfold increase in field magnitude moves xm inward by a factor of two and doubles Δφ in this planar model. Both trends make the barrier easier to cross, while the model’s microscopic limits remain important.

Practice

1. Why should the classical formula not be extrapolated to x = 0?

Inspect its inverse-distance behavior and underlying material model.

The continuum ideal-plane approximation gives a divergent interaction. Atomic structure, screening and interface bonding determine the near-interface physics there.
